Offline embedding refresh jobs are scheduled batch processes that regenerate vector embeddings for a corpus when the underlying embedding model changes or source documents update in bulk. They represent a deliberate operational choice to batch-refresh embeddings rather than update them on-demand or in real time.

## Process Model

These jobs typically:

- **Run on a fixed cadence** rather than on-demand, following a predetermined schedule
- **Re-embed** the full or incremental document set, depending on scope (wholesale model migration vs. incremental document updates)
- **Swap new vectors atomically** into the retrieval index to avoid serving mixed-model results during transition

The atomic swap ensures consistency: queries will not retrieve results from a mix of old and new embedding models, which would degrade search quality and make debugging difficult.

## Operational Concerns

### Model Versioning

Each batch should version the embedding model it uses. This is critical for:

- Tracing which model produced which vectors (essential when debugging quality regressions)
- Recovering the ability to revert if the new model underperforms
- Labeling vectors in the index so operators know the provenance of the data they are serving

### Vector Drift Monitoring

When old and new vectors coexist during a transition, or when batch results are being validated pre-swap, monitoring drift—the degree to which new vectors differ from old ones—helps detect:

- Silent quality regressions (new model produces similar-looking but less useful vectors)
- Model training errors or misconfiguration
- Whether a staged rollout is safe to proceed

### Staging and Rollback

A common implementation pattern is **blue/green indexing**:

- The **blue index** serves production queries
- The **green index** receives the new embedding batch and is validated offline
- Once quality checks pass, traffic is switched from blue to green
- The old blue index remains available for quick rollback if a regression is discovered post-swap

This staging approach gives operators an escape hatch if the new model underperforms in production, without requiring a full re-embedding run.

## Comparison to Alternatives

| Approach | When to use | Trade-offs |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| **Offline batch refresh** | Model change or bulk document update; predictable load | Lag between model/source change and production effect; planning/scheduling overhead |
| **On-demand refresh** | Urgent fixes; single-document update | Expensive; difficult to scale; can block user requests |
| **Real-time / streaming** | Continuous corpus refresh (e.g. high-volume document ingestion) | Higher operational complexity; resource usage tied to ingestion rate |
